{
  "need": "Status",
  "secondary": { "name": "Identity" },
  "read": "When a newer, younger person outpaces their manager in a visible skill, the status dynamic runs both directions. Your employee knows you know, and that creates a charged moment for them: do they hide it, tone it down, or push into it? The identity piece is live too, because they are actively figuring out where this talent fits in their professional story and how boldly to claim it.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Enforcer", "instinct": "The tempting move is to quietly reassert authority by steering them away from the area where they shine, or by over-explaining why experience still trumps raw skill. It signals insecurity on your end and shrinks them in the process, which poisons trust fast." },
  "mentorMove": "Name the gap openly and with genuine respect, then deliberately give them meaningful ownership in that domain. You hold the standard for the whole role while handing them real authority in the area where they are already ahead. That is not a threat to your credibility; it builds it.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "The standard for professional conduct and team accountability still applies to everyone, including this person.",
    "Their strong skill does not exempt them from the parts of the job they have not mastered yet."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "Let them lead, present, or own deliverables in the area where they excel rather than routing that work through you.",
    "Be open about learning from them directly; model the kind of professional curiosity you want them to carry through their whole career."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 2, "label": "Questions" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, I want to have a straight conversation with you about something I think is actually a good problem to have. Do you have ten minutes?" },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "I have been watching your work on the data modeling side, and honestly, you are further along there than I am. I am curious how you think about that part of the job and where you want to take it." },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Here is what I am thinking. I want to structure things so you have real ownership in that area, not just as support to me but as the person who drives it. I also need you fully engaged in the parts of the role you are still building, because that is where the whole picture comes together. Can we map out what that actually looks like?" },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I will be straight with you: I hold everyone on this team to a high standard across the full scope of the role, and I am holding you to the same bar. I am doing that because I think you can carry it, including the parts that are harder right now. The skill you already have is real, and I want us to build around it, not around it." }
  ],
  "longGame": "The way you handle this moment will define whether this person sees you as someone worth learning the rest of the craft from, or just an obstacle to route around. Managers who can say out loud that a direct report has surpassed them in something, and then give that person room to run, earn a kind of respect that outlasts any technical gap. That is the relationship that makes them stay and grow rather than leave to find space somewhere else."
}
situation: My newest hire is better at part of the job than I am and we both know it.
